title: Sputnik's Beep (1957)
voice_direction: Daniel or Mark Vale: steady, dry, unhurried. Matter-of-fact on the hook (slightly wry on 'shouldn't have frightened anyone'), a beat of quiet on 'the signal stopped', last line almost under the breath as a genuine question.
narration: This shiny ball held almost nothing but a radio, and it shouldn't have frightened anyone. Sputnik one was barely two feet wide when the Soviet Union launched it on the fourth of October, nineteen fifty-seven. Its only job was to beep, on two shortwave frequencies that any amateur radio operator could tune in. Most people who looked up at a bright light in the sky were probably seeing its rocket stage, not the ball. The beeps were not empty, either. Their length changed if the inside got too hot or too cold. After about three weeks, the batteries died, and the signal stopped. But the fear outlasted the signal. Within months, Washington had created ARPA, and then NASA. A beeping ball had started a race. Would you have been afraid?

instagram_caption:
This shiny ball held almost nothing but a radio, and it shouldn't have frightened anyone.

Sputnik 1 launched on 4 October 1957. It was a polished sphere about 58 cm wide, and its main payload was a radio sending beeps on 20 and 40 MHz that amateur radio operators could pick up.

Many people who looked up at a bright light in the sky were probably seeing the rocket's core stage, which was far brighter than the ball itself.

The beeps carried a little data too: their length changed if the temperature inside went out of range. On 26 October, after about three weeks, the batteries ran out and the signal stopped.

By then the alarm was in Washington. ARPA followed in February 1958 and NASA in July. One 1957 analyst found little sign of panic among the public.

facts.claim: Sputnik 1 launched 4 Oct 1957; transmitters on 20.005 and 40.002 MHz, 0.3 s pulses alternating between the two
facts.source: Wikipedia 'Sputnik 1' citing Zak/RussianSpaceWeb and RGANTD document; NASA NSSDC

facts.claim: Sphere about 58 cm (23 in) wide = 'barely two feet'. (58 cm figure from NSSDC/Wikipedia; not re-fetched here)
Amateur radio operators could receive the signals (ARRL 'Sputnik and Amateur Radio'); Kaminski received them in Bochum on a Hallicrafters-type station on display in Bonn
Most watchers saw the 26 m R-7 core stage (first magnitude), while the polished ball was ~6th magnitude, barely visible
facts.source: Wikipedia 'Sputnik 1' citing Brzezinski, Lafleur 2004, Bessonov 2007 Moscow News (hedged 'probably')

facts.claim: Pulse duration changed if internal temperature went above 50 C or below 0 C (and on pressure loss below 130 kPa); fan thermal switches 20-36 C
Transmitter batteries ran out 26 Oct 1957 (22 days; planned ~2 weeks); orbit decayed 4 Jan 1958 after 1,440 orbits
facts.source: Wikipedia 'Sputnik 1' citing AP/Argus-Leader 26 Oct 1957 and NASA NSSDC

facts.claim: ARPA authorised Feb 1958 (later DARPA); National Aeronautics and Space Act signed 29 Jul 1958 creating NASA; analyst Samuel Lubell found no evidence of public panic, so fear was largely elite
facts.source: Wikipedia 'Sputnik crisis' citing Launius (NASA 2005); NASA History

facts.claim: NACA's final meeting 21 Aug 1958 (Commons/NASA image description)

audio_recording.notes: Candidate only, authenticity NOT confirmed. Commons has a sibling file 'Possible PDM signal labeled as Sputnik by NASA.ogg' whose note says NASA NSSDC's 'Sputnik' sound is NOT the Sputnik-1 signal. Could not confirm Sputnik_beep.ogg is the authentic signal (NASA pages were blocked for fetch). Recommend synthesising a labelled recreation (0.3 s tone pairs alternating, ~3 Hz, shortwave static) and captioning it 'recreation'.
